extracted.intended_audience: travellers, campers, yachtsmen, Boy Scouts, and others who handle ropes
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and standards for making, joining, shortening, and otherwise handling ropes: selecting rope, choosing appropriate knots/hitches/bridles/eyes, and finishing (whipping, seizings, splices, grommets). Aims at safe, secure, and serviceable ropework for seafaring and outdoor uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whip or seize rope ends before working
rubrics_metrics.description: Before commencing work the loose ends or strands of a rope should be 'whipped' or 'seized' to prevent the rope from unravelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a piece of twine laid an inch or two from the end, pass the twine several times around the rope keeping the ends under the first few turns, make a large loop with the free end, continue winding for three or four turns around both rope and end of twine, then draw the loop tight by pulling the free end. Though an expert can work with loose-ended rope, it is a wise practice to invariably whip the end of every rope, cable, or hawser to be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and use correct rope terminology/parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'standing part', 'bight', and 'end' correctly when handling and describing knots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing Part = principal/longest portion; Bight = bent/curved part while working; End = part used to form the knot. Proper understanding aids correct tying and instruction-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the appropriate knot type for the task
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose knots according to purpose—temporary fastenings (bends/hitches), splices for smooth joins, stopper knots to prevent passing through an eye, shortenings for reducing length, decorative knots for ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match knot characteristics (security, ease of untying, bulk, how it bears strain, suitability for rope size/material) to task requirements rather than relying on a single favorite knot for all jobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square (Reef) knot as general-purpose joining knot
rubrics_metrics.description: The square knot is probably the most useful and widely used of common knots and is the best all-around knot known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make using the 'Left over, Right over' formula to avoid the Granny. It is very strong, never slips or becomes jammed, and is readily untied. Caveat: not reliable for tying two ropes of unequal size together; will frequently slip under such conditions unless the ends are seized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Granny knot
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Granny' is a poor and deceptive makeshift and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the proper sequence for the square/reef knot ('Left over, Right over') to prevent forming a granny knot which is useless and bothersome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Overhand and Figure‑Eight as stopper/utility knots
rubrics_metrics.description: Overhand and figure-eight knots are simple basic knots used for stopping ends, fastening yarns/strands in splicing, whipping, and seizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They form the basis for other knots; variations like double figure‑eight can prevent running through eyes or blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Open‑hand Knot for joining unequal-diameter ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: A better way to join two ropes of unequal diameter is to use the 'Open-hand Knot'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-hand knot never slips or gives but is large and clumsy; under great strain the rope is more likely to break at the knot than elsewhere. Prefer this to reef knot for unequal ropes; seize ends if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fisherman's Knot for small lines and anglers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fisherman's Knot—two simple overhand knots slipped over each rope and drawn taut—is valuable for anglers and for joining fine lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For gut lines leave the knot slightly open and wrap the space between with silk. It is probably the strongest known method for fastening fine lines and allows lines to be drawn apart by the ends for adding a third line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garrick Bend for heavy or stiff ropes/hawsers
rubrics_metrics.description: When joining two heavy or stiff ropes or hawsers the Garrick Bend is preeminently the best knot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form as illustrated; if the lines are very stiff or heavy secure the knot by seizing the ends to the standing parts. Avoid simple hitches within a loop (inferior) for heavy ropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half‑hitch and seizing for secure long joins
rubrics_metrics.description: For two heavy lines to be fastened for considerable time, use 'Half-hitch and Seizing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is secure, allows the rope to be handled more easily, and permits passing around winches or coiling better than some other knots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Lark's Head with toggle for instantly releasable ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Lark's Head with a marline‑spike or toggle is an easy tie that may be released instantly by removing the toggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass a bight through the ring or object, put a toggle through the sides of the bight and under/behind the standing part; end can be laid over and under the standing part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Slippery Hitch for quick-release fastening
rubrics_metrics.description: The Slippery Hitch is made by running the end through a ring or eye, back over the standing part, and pulling a bight through the loop; to untie, pull the free end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful where rapid unfastening is required; not for permanent or high-security needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two half‑hitches as a simple, reliable fastening
rubrics_metrics.description: Two half-hitches around a post, timber, or the standing part make an ideal and quickly tied fastening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be formed almost instantly; holds indefinitely without loosening and resists great strain even on smooth surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clove Hitch (Builder's Hitch) for securing to spars/posts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clove Hitch is a valuable knot for fastening to a spar or timber; will hold on a smooth timber and is used by builders for staging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Made by passing the end around the spar, over itself, over and around again, and tucking end under itself. With ends knotted becomes the Gunner's Knot. For towing or hauling timber a Timber Hitch may be superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber Hitch for towing and securing hawsers to spars/logs
rubrics_metrics.description: Timber Hitch is easily made by passing the end around the spar, round the standing part, and twisting three or more times around under/over itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For extra security add a single half-hitch a couple of feet further along the spar. It is often better than the Clove Hitch for towing logs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Catspaw for hoisting on hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catspaw is a useful hitch for hoisting with a hook and is formed by making bights and taking three twists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form a bight over the hook, take three twists away from you, bring the two bights side by side and throw over the hook. Good for hoisting without damaging the rope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackwall Hitch as a quick temporary jam on a hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackwall Hitch is a simple loop with the end passed underneath the standing part and across the hook so pressure jams the end against the hook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very quick and easy but likely to jam under great pressure; mainly useful for light or temporary work like packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain Hitch for hauling large ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain Hitch consists of a series of half-hitches taken at intervals around an object and is strong for hauling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to help haul a large rope or for similar purposes; can be used with a lever or handspike for mechanical advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling Hitch, Magnus Hitch, Studding‑sail Bend for specialty uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolling Hitch, Magnus Hitch, and Studding‑sail Bend are modifications or specific hitches used in shipboard and spar-handling situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn these when applicable to the particular task (holding on spars, controlling loads, setting studding sails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bowline as the essential sailor's knot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bowline is a sailor's knot par excellence; it never slips, jams, or fails, is easily and quickly untied, and is useful in many places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the tying sequence (form a bight, pass end through, under, over, and through, then draw taut). Variants include Bowline on a Bight (for slinging casks or forming a seat) and Running Bowline (slip knot form). Bowline should be preferred for secure non-jamming loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Bowline loops over other loop knots where safety is critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Other loops exist but none are as safe, sure, and useful as the Bowline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bowline or its appropriate variant for slinging, lowering men, or making secure loops; avoid less reliable loops for safety-critical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct shortenings for taking up spare rope
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortenings (double, treble, fourfold knots, single plait/monkey chain, double chain/twist braid, open chain) are used to reduce rope length and tidy spare rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose shortening by need: some are quick-release (single plait/monkey chain undone by removing toggle), others are more permanent and should have ends fastened; use seized ends if rope must bear strain or be permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheepshank forms for shortening centre of a tied rope
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheepshank (Dogshank) is widely used for shortening rope, especially when both ends are fast; several forms exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best and most secure sheepshank form involves a running knot with bends pushed through loops; a simpler form can be used if ends are seized. Some sheepshanks include toggles for quick release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grommet construction rule: strand length = five times circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: A grommet is formed of a single strand of rope five times as long as the circumference of the grommet when complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay one end across the other at desired size, follow the lay of the strand until back to start to form two-strand ring, then continue until three-strand ring is complete; secure ends with overhand knots, pass ends under nearest strands and trim. Keep a strong twist while 'laying up' for a firm smooth endless ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make selvedgee straps, Flemish eyes, and artificial eyes properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Selvagee straps (made on pins/nails and seized), Flemish eyes (made over a spar using yarns and whipping), and Artificial eyes (unlaying one strand and following around) are methods to create handles/eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the stepwise construction: lay yarns around a former, lap and tie as directed, whip the finished eye all around to finish neatly. For artificial eye, unlay one strand, follow around the spaces between remaining strands and finish by tapering and whipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use throat seizing and lashed cut‑splice for certain eyes and rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Throat seizing and lashed cut-splices are methods for making eyes or rings when a splice is not required or desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open the end slightly and lash it to the standing part for a throat seizing; lash two ends of a short rope to the standing part to form a ring; cuckold's necks with lashings/clinches also serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use splices when a smooth, even surface is required for joined ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Splices are used in many cases to join ropes so they present a smooth and even surface; knots are for temporary fastenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer splices (short splice, long splice, eye/cut splices) when joined rope needs to run through blocks, over drums, or present an even lay; knots can cause bulk or points of weakness for such uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select rope material and construction appropriate to use; understand strength/weight formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Rope strength depends on fibre strength/length, amount of twist, and preparation; rope construction (yarns→strands→rope→cable) and lay direction matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough strength estimate: multiply circumference in inches by itself and take one-fifth of the product to get number of tons the rope will sustain (example: 5

rubrics_metrics.name: keep rope construction opposed twists
rubrics_metrics.description: When making strands, yarns are twisted opposite to fibres, strands are twisted opposite to yarns, and ropes opposite to strands so natural untwisting tendencies bind the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three‑stranded rope usually turns 'with the sun' (right‑hand); cables left‑handed. Understand lay to choose correct splicing and working methods.
